paragraphs.text: [Ya Shi Xiang](dancong:ya-shi-xiang) (鸭屎香), named for duck dung, is the market name for one line of [Phoenix Dancong](dancong:definition), the [oolong](oolong:definition) of Phoenix Mountain. The line is traced to Pingkengtou village. Three stories explain the name, and all are told only as stories: that it was chosen to keep thieves away from the bush, that it comes from the yellow local earth called duck dung soil, and that duck droppings lay on the bush. A second name, Yinhua Xiang, silver flower, was put forward in 2014, though many sellers keep the old one.

Phoenix Mountain, [Fenghuang Shan](phoenix-mountain:where-it-is), is a range in Chao'an district of Chaozhou, in eastern Guangdong, with tea on its slopes up to roughly 1,100 metres. Cloud and mist sit on the upper slopes for much of the year and the nights are cool, so the bushes grow slowly. The higher the garden, the more a tea from it is expected to show what the trade calls [mountain rhyme](phoenix-mountain:mist-and-climate).

As with all Dancong, the leaf is withered in the sun, then [shaken and rested in rounds](dancong:making) to bruise its edges, fixed at high heat, rolled into long strips and roasted as it is refined. This is a 2026 tea. Freshly roasted Dancong is [rested for some months](dancong:ageing) before it is drunk, and it keeps sealed, dry, cool and out of the light.

brewing.text: Brew it gongfu style in a small gaiwan or clay pot, with about 3 to 8 grams for 100 to 120 ml and hot water, about 88 to 100°C; Chinese accounts mostly say 95 to 100°C. A quick rinse is common. Steeps start at a few seconds and grow a few seconds each round, and a good Dancong gives about eight to fifteen. Too long, too hot or too much leaf and it turns bitter and astringent.

notice.text: Flowers above all, a sweetness that comes back after swallowing, a high scent that lasts, honey, often ripe fruit such as peach, and what the trade calls mountain rhyme, shan yun; a liquor from golden to orange-red or amber.
